# Introduction

This analysis explores the UCI **Absenteeism at Work** dataset (740 absence
records from 36 employees at a Brazilian courier company). It follows the
CRISP-DM process: understand the data, explore it, then cluster it to answer
two questions — *what kinds of absences happen here?* and *what kinds of
employees do we have?*

The main finding, previewed up front: absence **duration** is driven mostly by
the medical reason, while what separates employees is absence **frequency** —
and higher frequency is strongly associated with social drinking.

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)   # data wrangling + ggplot2
library(janitor)     # clean_names()
library(skimr)       # skim() summaries
library(corrplot)    # correlation heatmap
library(cluster)     # daisy() (Gower distance) + pam()
```

# Data ingestion

The file is **semicolon-delimited**, so we read it with `read_delim(delim = ";")`.
`clean_names()` then tidies the messy column names (trailing spaces, slashes)
into snake_case.

```{r ingest}
# The path is relative to this R/ folder (knitting runs from here)
raw <- read_delim(
  "../data/Absenteeism_at_work.csv",
  delim = ";",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

abs <- clean_names(raw)
glimpse(abs)
```

**Output:** 740 rows, 21 columns. Note every column reads as numeric (`<dbl>`),
even though many are really categories in disguise (reason codes, day of week,
yes/no flags). We fix that next.

# Data preparation: recode categories as factors

Many columns are *labels stored as numbers* — e.g. `day_of_the_week` uses codes
2–6 for Mon–Fri. Treating them as numbers would let R do nonsense arithmetic
("Thursday minus Monday = 3"). Converting them to **factors** tells R they are
categories, not quantities.

```{r recode}
abs <- abs %>%
  mutate(
    id = factor(id),   # an employee label, never a quantity

    day_of_the_week = factor(day_of_the_week,
                             levels = c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
                             labels = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri")),

    seasons = factor(seasons,
                     levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
                     labels = c("Summer", "Autumn", "Winter", "Spring")),

    education = factor(education,
                       levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
                       labels = c("High school", "Graduate",
                                  "Postgraduate", "Master/Doctor")),

    # Binary flags: 0/1 -> No/Yes
    disciplinary_failure = factor(disciplinary_failure, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    social_drinker       = factor(social_drinker,       levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    social_smoker        = factor(social_smoker,        levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),

    # Kept as plain factor codes (no custom labels)
    reason_for_absence = factor(reason_for_absence),
    month_of_absence   = factor(month_of_absence)
  )

glimpse(abs)
```

Quick check that the recoding took — the factor levels and a tally of one:

```{r recode-check}
levels(abs$day_of_the_week)   # allowed categories, in order
table(abs$day_of_the_week)    # count of absences per weekday
```

# Data understanding (EDA)

## Overview summaries

`summary()` and `skim()` give a first look at every column — type-appropriate
stats for numbers, category counts for factors.

```{r summaries}
summary(abs)
skim(abs)
```

## Data-quality checks

Two hidden issues to catch before analysis.

**Issue 1 — impossible months.** Month should be 1–12; a `0` bucket is a
data-entry error.

```{r quality-month}
table(abs$month_of_absence)
```

**Issue 2 — zero-hour "absences".** These turn out to be disciplinary records
(reason 0, disciplinary_failure = Yes), not real absences.

```{r quality-zero}
table(abs$absenteeism_time_in_hours == 0)

abs %>%
  filter(absenteeism_time_in_hours == 0) %>%
  count(reason_for_absence, disciplinary_failure)
```

**Output:** 44 zero-hour rows, ~40 of them disciplinary. These aren't absences,
so we drop them — a scope decision (analyse *genuine* absences), not just a
data-quality fix.

## Cleaning

```{r clean}
abs_clean <- abs %>%
  filter(month_of_absence != 0) %>%        # drop 3 broken-month rows
  filter(absenteeism_time_in_hours > 0)    # keep only genuine absences (>0 hrs)

nrow(abs)         # 740 (original, untouched)
nrow(abs_clean)   # 696 (the month-0 rows were a subset of the zero-hour rows)
```

**Note:** we land on 696, not 693 — the 3 month-0 rows were *already* zero-hour
rows, so the two filters overlap completely. Bad records cluster together.

# Exploring the target: absence hours

The target is heavily right-skewed (a few very long absences), so we view it on
a `log(1 + x)` scale to see the structure. `log1p` is used (not `log`) because
it is safe at zero.

```{r target-hist}
ggplot(abs_clean, aes(x = log1p(absenteeism_time_in_hours))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "darkorange", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Absence hours on a log(1 + x) scale — the skew flattens out",
       x = "log(1 + absence hours)", y = "Number of records") +
  theme_minimal()

summary(abs_clean$absenteeism_time_in_hours)
```

**Output:** median 3h, mean 7.4h. Mean far above median = strong right skew.
The tallest spike is at 8 hours — a full workday off.

# What drives absence duration?

## By reason for absence

```{r reason-boxplot}
ggplot(abs_clean, aes(x = reason_for_absence, y = absenteeism_time_in_hours)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Absence duration varies a lot by reason",
       x = "Reason for absence (ICD code)", y = "Absence time (hours)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Reason clearly matters — but before trusting any single box, check how many
absences sit behind it (a dramatic box built on 4 rows is noise).

```{r reason-counts}
abs_clean %>%
  count(reason_for_absence, sort = TRUE) %>%
  print(n = 27)
```

**Output:** routine reasons dominate (23 medical consultation = 149, 28 dental
= 112, 27 physiotherapy = 68), while several dramatic-looking reasons have
< 5 absences. So we re-plot using only reasons with **10+** absences, ordered
by median duration:

```{r reason-boxplot-clean}
common_reasons <- abs_clean %>%
  count(reason_for_absence) %>%
  filter(n >= 10) %>%
  pull(reason_for_absence)

abs_clean %>%
  filter(reason_for_absence %in% common_reasons) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(reason_for_absence, absenteeism_time_in_hours, FUN = median),
             y = absenteeism_time_in_hours)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Absence duration by reason (reasons with 10+ absences)",
       subtitle = "Ordered by median; rare reasons excluded to avoid over-reading noise",
       x = "Reason for absence (ICD code)", y = "Absence time (hours)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Output:** routine care (dental, physiotherapy, consultation) → short; injury
and musculoskeletal → longer and more variable.

## Do the numeric variables relate to duration?

Correlation measures straight-line association between numbers. We compute it
between absence hours and every numeric suspect, then rank.

```{r correlation}
numeric_suspects <- abs_clean %>%
  select(absenteeism_time_in_hours, age, service_time, work_load_average_day,
         transportation_expense, distance_from_residence_to_work, hit_target,
         son, pet, weight, height, body_mass_index)

cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_suspects)

sort(cor_matrix[, "absenteeism_time_in_hours"], decreasing = TRUE)
```

**Output:** every correlation is under 0.15 — essentially no linear relationship.
Duration is not driven by any single number (age, distance, workload, BMI...).
That's a real finding: the signal lives in the *categories*, not the numbers.

We double-check the least-weak one (`son`) as categories, in case a curve was
hiding that correlation missed:

```{r son-boxplot}
abs_clean %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(son), y = absenteeism_time_in_hours)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Absence duration by number of children",
       x = "Number of children", y = "Absence time (hours)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Output:** flat across all groups — confirms no relationship.

## Do the other categories relate to duration?

We reshape to long format (`pivot_longer`) so we can facet all categorical
suspects into one consolidated plot.

```{r facet}
abs_long <- abs_clean %>%
  select(absenteeism_time_in_hours, day_of_the_week, seasons,
         social_drinker, social_smoker, education) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(day_of_the_week, seasons, social_drinker, social_smoker, education),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  )

ggplot(abs_long, aes(x = value, y = absenteeism_time_in_hours)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Absence duration across the categorical suspects",
       x = NULL, y = "Absence time (hours)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

**Output:** all five panels are flat. Day, season, education, drinker, smoker —
none change absence *duration*. Combined with the flat correlations, this cements
it: **duration is driven by the medical reason and little else.**

# Absence frequency: a different question

Duration plots are blind to *how often* someone is absent. So we aggregate to
one row per employee and look at frequency instead.

```{r freq}
freq <- abs_clean %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(n_absences = n(),
            total_hours = sum(absenteeism_time_in_hours),
            .groups = "drop")

arrange(freq, desc(n_absences))

ggplot(freq, aes(x = n_absences)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Absence frequency varies widely across employees",
       x = "Number of absences", y = "Employees") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Output:** very uneven — a few employees absent constantly, most rarely.

Now attach fixed traits and test whether they relate to frequency.

```{r freq2}
freq2 <- abs_clean %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(n_absences = n(),
            social_drinker = first(social_drinker),
            social_smoker  = first(social_smoker),
            age = first(age),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(freq2, aes(x = social_drinker, y = n_absences)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Absence frequency by drinker status",
       x = "Social drinker", y = "Number of absences") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(freq2, aes(x = social_smoker, y = n_absences)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Absence frequency by smoker status",
       x = "Social smoker", y = "Number of absences") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(freq2, aes(x = age, y = n_absences)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "darkorange") +
  labs(title = "Absence frequency vs age", x = "Age", y = "Number of absences") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Always check group sizes before trusting a split:

```{r freq-counts}
freq2 %>% count(social_smoker)
freq2 %>% count(social_drinker)
```

**Output:** drinkers (16 No / 17 Yes) are balanced — the drinker split is
**credible**, and drinkers are absent more often. Smokers (only 7 Yes) are too
few to trust. Age trend is weak and outlier-driven. So: **drinking relates to
higher frequency; that's the one solid frequency lead.**

# Clustering 1 — kinds of absences (absence-level)

We cluster the 696 absences. Because the data is **mixed** (numbers + categories),
k-means won't work — it can only do arithmetic on numbers. We use **Gower
distance** (handles mixed types) fed into **PAM** (k-means's cousin that accepts
a distance matrix).

```{r clust-prep}
clust_data <- abs_clean %>%
  select(reason_for_absence, month_of_absence, day_of_the_week, seasons,
         absenteeism_time_in_hours, transportation_expense,
         distance_from_residence_to_work, age,
         social_drinker, social_smoker, education)

str(clust_data)   # confirm factors are factors, numbers are numbers
```

```{r gower}
gower_dist <- daisy(clust_data, metric = "gower")
summary(gower_dist)   # Gower distances fall between 0 and 1
```

## Choosing k (silhouette)

Try k = 2–8; higher silhouette width = better-separated clusters.

```{r sil-absence}
sil_width <- numeric(8)
for (k in 2:8) {
  pam_fit <- pam(gower_dist, diss = TRUE, k = k)
  sil_width[k] <- pam_fit$silinfo$avg.width
}

plot(2:8, sil_width[2:8], type = "b",
     xlab = "Number of clusters (k)", ylab = "Average silhouette width",
     main = "Higher = better-separated clusters")
```

**Output:** all scores are low (~0.14) — absences do **not** form crisp types.
We take k = 2 (interpretable) and report the weak separation honestly.

## Fit and profile (k = 2)

```{r pam-absence}
pam_fit <- pam(gower_dist, diss = TRUE, k = 2)

abs_clustered <- clust_data %>%
  mutate(cluster = as.factor(pam_fit$clustering))

table(abs_clustered$cluster)   # ~351 / 345, an even split

abs_clustered %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            avg_hours    = mean(absenteeism_time_in_hours),
            avg_age      = mean(age),
            avg_distance = mean(distance_from_residence_to_work),
            avg_expense  = mean(transportation_expense))
```

What defines the split — drinker and education (as proportions):

```{r absence-profile}
abs_clustered %>%
  count(cluster, social_drinker) %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n))

abs_clustered %>%
  count(cluster, education) %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n))
```

**Output:** the two clusters split almost entirely on **drinker status**
(cluster 1 ≈ 78% non-drinkers, cluster 2 ≈ 91% drinkers), with education and
distance tracking along. These traits travel together.

## Sanity check — do clusters map to employees?

Since 696 absences come from 33 people, the split may really be a *people* split.

```{r absence-sanity}
check <- abs_clean %>%
  mutate(cluster = as.factor(pam_fit$clustering))

check %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(n_absences = n(),
            pct_cluster1 = mean(cluster == 1),   # 1 = all in cluster 1, 0 = all in cluster 2
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(n_absences))
```

**Output:** mostly (not purely) about people — the highest-volume employees sit
almost entirely in one cluster, but a few employees split across both. So the
clusters are largely an employee split, with some genuine absence-level variation.

# Clustering 2 — kinds of employees (employee-level)

Absence-level clustering is blind to *frequency*. Aggregating to 33 employees
lets us cluster on frequency + severity, which surfaces a segmentation the
absence-level model couldn't.

```{r emp-build}
emp_data <- abs_clean %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_absences  = n(),                              # FREQUENCY
    avg_hours   = mean(absenteeism_time_in_hours),  # SEVERITY
    total_hours = sum(absenteeism_time_in_hours),   # total burden
    age         = first(age),
    distance    = first(distance_from_residence_to_work),
    drinker     = first(social_drinker),
    smoker      = first(social_smoker),
    education   = first(education),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

emp_data
```

```{r emp-gower}
emp_features <- emp_data %>% select(-id)   # drop id for the distance calc
gower_emp <- daisy(emp_features, metric = "gower")

sil_emp <- numeric(8)
for (k in 2:8) {
  pam_k <- pam(gower_emp, diss = TRUE, k = k)
  sil_emp[k] <- pam_k$silinfo$avg.width
}
plot(2:8, sil_emp[2:8], type = "b",
     xlab = "k", ylab = "Avg silhouette width",
     main = "Employee clustering: how many segments?")
```

**Output:** silhouette ~0.33 — **much** cleaner than the absence-level 0.14.
Fewer, cleaner rows separate better than many noisy ones. We choose k = 3
(near the peak, and interpretable).

## Fit and profile (k = 3)

```{r emp-pam}
pam_emp <- pam(gower_emp, diss = TRUE, k = 3)

emp_data <- emp_data %>%
  mutate(segment = as.factor(pam_emp$clustering))

emp_data %>%
  group_by(segment) %>%
  summarise(
    n_employees    = n(),
    avg_n_absences = mean(n_absences),   # frequency
    avg_hours_each = mean(avg_hours),    # severity
    avg_total_hrs  = mean(total_hours),  # total burden
    avg_age        = mean(age),
    avg_distance   = mean(distance)
  )

emp_data %>%
  group_by(segment) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            pct_drinker  = mean(drinker == "Yes"),
            pct_smoker   = mean(smoker == "Yes"),
            avg_distance = mean(distance))
```

**Output:** three segments form a **frequency ladder** — low (~4 absences),
moderate (~20), high (~29) — while typical absence length stays ~8h across all
three. So employees differ by *how often*, not *how long*. And the traits track
perfectly: the high-frequency segment is 100% drinkers, the moderate segment 0%.
The drinker signal appears a third time (after the frequency boxplots and the
absence-level clustering) — strong corroboration in a 33-person sample.
```{r}
abs_clustered <- abs_clean %>%
  mutate(
    cluster = as.factor(pam_fit$clustering),
    cluster_name = case_when(
      cluster == 1 ~ "Profile A",
      cluster == 2 ~ "Profile B"
    ))
```


```{r}
emp_data <- emp_data %>%
  mutate(
    segment_name = case_when(
      segment == 1 ~ "Moderate",
      segment == 2 ~ "Low absence",
      segment == 3 ~ "High burden"
    ))
```


```{r}
abs <- abs %>%
  mutate(
    reason_label = case_when(
      reason_for_absence == 23 ~ "Medical consultation",
      reason_for_absence == 28 ~ "Dental consultation",
      reason_for_absence == 27 ~ "Physiotherapy",
      reason_for_absence == 13 ~ "Musculoskeletal",
      reason_for_absence == 19 ~ "Injury / poisoning",
      reason_for_absence == 22 ~ "Follow-up medical",
      reason_for_absence == 26 ~ "Unjustified absence",
      reason_for_absence == 25 ~ "Lab exam / referral",
      reason_for_absence == 11 ~ "Digestive system",
      reason_for_absence == 10 ~ "Respiratory system",
      TRUE ~ "Other"    # everything not listed above
    )
  )
```

# Save outputs for Power BI

```{r save}
dir.create("../output", showWarnings = FALSE)   # make the folder if it isn't there yet

write_csv(abs,            "../output/absenteeism_full_labelled.csv")   # 740 rows, all labelled — for the EDA page
write_csv(abs_clustered,  "../output/absenteeism_clustered.csv")       # now WITH id + cluster_name
write_csv(emp_data,       "../output/employee_segments.csv")           # now WITH segment_name
```

# Findings summary

- **Duration** is driven mainly by the **medical reason**; numeric variables and
  most categories are flat.
- **Frequency** is where employees differ — a small reliable group, a moderate
  group, and a high-burden group that drives most lost time.
- Higher frequency is **strongly associated with social drinking** (seen three
  independent ways). Association only — small, entangled sample; not causation.
- **Absence-level clusters** are weak (they don't form crisp types);
  **employee-level segments** are much cleaner and more actionable.

*Caveat throughout: 740 absences come from just 33 employees, so person-level
findings rest on a small sample — clear tendencies, not population law.*
